narrative:
The model determined that you have a 39% chance of representing a bad credit risk. Because this probability is high enough to cross the bank's approval threshold, your loan application was denied.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this outcome were the status of your checking account, the purpose of the loan, and the presence of a co-applicant. Your checking account has no balance, which is the single biggest reason the application was turned down. Among approved applicants, only 59% have no checking account; the bank sees an empty or unknown account as a warning sign that tilts the decision heavily toward risk. 

The fact that you are requesting the money to buy a new car also pushed the prediction toward denial. While new-car loans are fairly common, the model views this purpose as less favorable than requests for items such as furniture or home electronics that approved borrowers more often seek.

Having a co-applicant, rather than applying alone, added a further increase in perceived risk, though this effect was smaller than the first two factors.

On the positive side, several aspects of your profile worked in your favor: you have been employed for seven years or more, you are requesting a relatively modest amount (well below the average of approved loans), and you own your home. Unfortunately these strengths were not enough to overcome the concerns raised by the top three issues.

You should consider re-applying after you have built up a visible balance in a checking account and, if possible, explore whether a different loan purpose would better align with what the bank prefers. Improving those areas would likely give you a stronger chance of approval.
